note: Which sliced reference figure stands for each of canon's nine classes.
Hand-authored, not generated: the strips in this directory are cut from the
reference sheets and carry the sheets' own labels (cleric, mage, rogue, warrior,
plus a `ranger` and an unlabelled `knight`), and canon has nine classes with no
Ranger and no Knight among them. Something has to decide, and the decision is
recorded here rather than hidden in a screen.
THE RULE: canon's EQUIPMENT FAMILIES decide, because a full figure shows what
it is wearing. data/classes.json groups the nine into four armour families —
warrior_bard_armor (warrior, bard), monk_rogue_armor (monk, rogue),
healer_armor (cleric, druid, shaman), mage_wizard_armor (mage, wizard) — and
the reference drew exactly four labelled figures. So each family gets one
figure's family of poses, and classes inside a family are told apart by pose
(`_b` is the sheets' second pose set for the same figure).
THIS DISAGREES WITH THE BUSTS, deliberately, and docs/15 BL-68 records it.
tools/art/derive_busts.py built the five portraits canon does not draw by
repainting the four it does, pairing monk<-warrior, druid<-rogue, bard<-mage,
shaman<-cleric. A bust is a face and a hat, so pairing by headgear is right for
a bust; a figure is armour, so pairing by armour family is right for a figure.
Monk, druid and bard therefore sit in different families here than their busts
were derived from, and that is the intended answer, not a mistake to reconcile.
THE ONE EXCEPTION: healer_armor has THREE classes and the reference drew TWO
healer poses. Shaman takes the unlabelled armoured figure, which is consistent
with what healer_armor means in canon — the cleric is a main-tank-healer in
plate — and with the shipped shaman bust, which is an armoured helm repainted
bone. Deriving a third healer strip by repaint was tried and rejected: the
bust's shaman recipe masks steel at s<0.25 and v>0.45, and these 30px figures
carry ~10% desaturated pixels at v=0.26, so the repaint would have been
invisible. The exception is declared to the test rather than worked around.

warrior.why: The sheets' own `warrior`. Canon's main tank in the family canon names for it.

bard.why: Shares warrior_bard_armor AND warrior_bard_head with the warrior, so the bard is a warrior-framed figure with an instrument, not a robed one. Second pose so the two read apart.

monk.why: Shares monk_rogue_armor with the rogue — canon dresses the monk in the rogue's leather, not the warrior's plate.

druid.why: Shares healer_armor with the cleric. The green `ranger` figure reads more druidic and is NOT used, because canon puts the druid in the healers' armour rather than in leather.

shaman.why: The declared exception: three healers, two healer poses. An armoured figure is what healer_armor means here, and the shipped shaman bust is an armoured helm repainted bone.

mage.why: The sheets' own `mage` — the blue hat and robe.

wizard.why: Shares mage_wizard_armor with the mage; second pose. The wizard is the mage grown old, which is how its bust was derived too.

unclaimed.ranger_as_rogue: Canon has no Ranger. Its green leather is closest to monk_rogue_armor, and both of that family's slots are taken by the figures the sheets labelled `rogue`. Kept for scene crowds.
unclaimed.ranger_as_rogue_b: Second pose of the same unclaimed figure.
unclaimed.knight_unlabelled_b: Second pose of the figure the shaman claims; a tenth class would take it.

family_exceptions.shaman: healer_armor has three classes and the reference drew two healer poses; see `note`.
